messages.content: You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
HELP there are tiny green bugs all over my flytrap and it looks awful

Those are aphids, and they are one of the most common flytrap pests. Spray with insecticidal soap or a horticultural soap spray, but test it on a single trap or leaf first and wait a day, since carnivorous plants can react badly to some products. Repeat the treatment after about a week to kill anything that hatches from eggs the first spray missed. Avoid any product that contains fertilizer or added nutrients, because those will burn the roots.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
White fuzzy bugs on my plant?

That is almost certainly mealybugs - they look like little blobs of cotton wool and hide in leaf joints and around the growth point. Insecticidal soap works well on them, applied so the spray actually reaches into the crevices where they cluster, and tested on one leaf first. Give it a second round about a week later, because mealybug eggs hatch in waves. Never use a systemic feed-and-protect product, since the fertilizer content is worse for the plant than the pest is.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
I found little brown bumps stuck to the stem of my Nepenthes that scrape off with a fingernail. What are they?

Those are scale insects, and the hard shell is why they shrug off a lot of sprays. Scrape or wipe off what you can with a cotton bud, then treat with insecticidal soap or a light horticultural oil, trying it on one leaf first to check the plant tolerates it. Scale needs persistence, so repeat weekly for several weeks to catch the mobile crawler stage. Keep the plant away from the rest of your collection until it is clean.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
my sundew leaves look kind of stippled and dusty and there's fine webbing between them

Fine webbing plus a pale stippled look means spider mites, which thrive in warm dry air. Raise the humidity, because mites hate damp conditions, and treat with insecticidal soap making sure to hit the undersides of the leaves where they live. Test the spray on one leaf first and repeat after about a week, since mite eggs are not killed by soap. Some growers instead submerge the whole plant in distilled water for a day or two, which drowns mites effectively.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
What are thrips and how do I get rid of them on carnivorous plants?

Thrips are slender insects barely a couple of millimetres long that rasp at new growth, leaving silvery scarring and distorted, stunted leaves. They are stubborn, so plan on repeated insecticidal soap treatments about a week apart rather than a single spray, and test on one leaf before doing the whole plant. Because they breed fast and hide in unopened growth, isolating the affected plant makes a real difference. Skip systemic products that include fertilizer - the nutrients will damage the roots.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
There are little black flies buzzing around the soil of all my plants. Are they hurting them?

Those are fungus gnats, and the adults are mostly a nuisance rather than a real threat - it is the larvae in the top layer of peat that can nibble at fine roots and seedlings. Letting the surface dry slightly between waterings makes the soil much less inviting, and yellow sticky traps knock the adult population down quickly. Improving air circulation with a small fan also helps. In an established flytrap or sundew pot, the plants will happily catch a fair number of them for you.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Something is eating chunks out of my Sarracenia pitchers outside at night

Ragged chewed edges appearing overnight usually mean slugs or snails, which will happily work their way through pitchers and traps. Go out after dark with a torch and pick them off by hand, and use physical barriers such as copper tape or grit around the pot rather than chemical baits. Many slug baits are salt based, and salts are exactly what you do not want anywhere near carnivorous plant roots. Clearing damp hiding places near the pots reduces the population over time.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
found a fat green caterpillar inside one of my pitcher plants, it had eaten right through the tube

Caterpillars, particularly the moth larvae that specialise in Sarracenia, will bore into a pitcher and hollow it out from the inside. Remove the caterpillar by hand and cut off the ruined pitcher below the damage so it does not rot on the plant. Check the other pitchers for entry holes, since one moth usually lays more than one egg. Hand picking is the safest control - it avoids putting any chemical on a plant that is sensitive to residues.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Ants keep marching in and out of my flytrap. Bad sign?

Ants are a mixed bag. Some get caught and eaten, which is fine, but large colonies will raid traps to steal the digesting prey and can even nest in the pot and dry out the root zone. If they are nesting, stand the pot in a tray of mineral-free water for a day or two, which usually persuades them to move out. Avoid ant baits and granules near the pot, because they are loaded with sugars and salts that do the soil no favours.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Is there any pesticide that is actually safe for carnivorous plants?

Insecticidal soap and plain horticultural soap sprays are the usual first choice, and most growers get good results with them. Whatever you pick, test it on one leaf or trap and wait a day or two before treating the entire plant, because carnivorous plants are noticeably more sensitive to sprays than ordinary houseplants. The absolute rule is to avoid anything that combines pest control with feeding, since the fertilizer in those products burns carnivorous plant roots. Repeat any treatment after about a week to break the pest life cycle.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How do I actually apply insecticidal soap? Do I spray everything?

Mix or buy it at the recommended strength and spray until the plant is wet all over, paying particular attention to leaf undersides, growth points and the tight crevices where pests hide. Do a patch test on a single leaf first and give it a day to make sure there is no scorching. It is best done out of direct sun and in the cooler part of the day so the solution does not bake onto the leaves. One application is rarely enough - go again roughly a week later to catch newly hatched insects.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
someone on a forum said to just dunk the whole plant underwater to kill bugs?? does that work

It does, and it is a well used trick. Submerge the entire plant, pot and all, in distilled or other mineral-free water for a day or two, and the pests drown for lack of air. It works particularly well for aphids and mites hiding in places a spray cannot reach, and it leaves no chemical residue on a sensitive plant. Use clean mineral-free water rather than tap water, and let the pot drain properly afterwards so the roots are not left sitting airless.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Why does everyone say not to use those systemic bug killer sticks or granules?

Most of those products are sold as combined feed-and-protect, and the fertilizer component is the problem. Carnivorous plants evolved in nutrient-poor bogs and their roots are burned by the mineral salts in ordinary plant food, so a product that fertilizes while it treats will often do more harm than the pest. If a systemic really is needed, it has to be one with no added nutrients at all. In practice, insecticidal soap or submersion handles nearly everything a home grower runs into.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Can I use neem oil on a Venus flytrap?

Plenty of growers do use neem successfully, but it is a product carnivorous plants can react to, so treat it as something to test rather than assume. Spray a single trap or leaf with a diluted solution, wait a day or two, and only continue if nothing browns or distorts. Apply out of direct sunlight, since oil plus strong sun can scorch foliage. Check the label carefully and reject any formulation that includes fertilizer or added nutrients.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Do I really need to quarantine a new plant if it looks clean?

Yes, because the pests that cause the most trouble are the ones you cannot see yet. Keep a new arrival separate from the rest of your collection for a few weeks and inspect it regularly, especially the undersides of leaves and the growth point. Scale, mites and mealybugs often show up only once eggs hatch, which is exactly why the waiting period matters. A few weeks of separation is far less work than treating an entire collection.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Grey fuzzy patches showing up on my flytrap leaves in the terrarium. What is it?

That is grey mould, usually Botrytis, and it takes hold where the air is still and everything stays permanently wet. Open the terrarium up or run a small fan to get air moving, and cut away the affected leaves along with any dead material and old digested prey, since decaying tissue is where it starts. Letting the soil surface dry slightly between waterings also slows it down. If it keeps recurring after the conditions are fixed, a sulphur-based fungicide will help.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
my nepenthes is wilting even though the soil is soaking wet

Wilting in wet soil is the classic picture of root rot, and Nepenthes are especially prone to it because they will not tolerate standing water the way flytraps and Sarracenia do. The problem is soil that is waterlogged and airless at the same time, so get the pot out of any tray, let it drain freely, and only water when the top of the mix feels barely damp. Repotting into a chunkier, more open mix often saves a plant if the roots are not too far gone. Keep it humid and shaded while it recovers and judge progress by whether new growth appears.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
The centre of my Venus flytrap has gone soft and mushy and brown. Is it dead?

A soft brown rhizome means crown rot, which normally follows from the crown staying wet with no air movement, often after dead leaves were left to decay around it. Clear away every scrap of dead material, improve the airflow around the plant, and stop overhead watering so the growth point can dry between soakings. If some firm white rhizome tissue remains you can cut back to it and repot into fresh mix, though recovery is not guaranteed. A sulphur-based fungicide is worth using if rot has been a repeating problem for you.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
There's white fuzzy mould growing all over the top of the peat. Should I panic?

Not panic, but do act, because surface mould is telling you the air is stagnant and the surface never dries. Get some air moving with a small fan or by opening the container, take out any dead leaves and leftover prey that are feeding it, and let the very top of the mix dry a little between waterings. Scraping off the worst of the fuzz helps in the short term. If it comes back repeatedly once conditions are improved, treat with a sulphur-based fungicide.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
I put my flytrap in the fridge for dormancy and now there's mould on it

Refrigerator dormancy is the situation where mould appears most often, because the bag is closed, the plant is damp and nothing is moving the air. Open the bag to let it breathe, trim off every dead or mouldy leaf, and make sure the medium is just damp rather than soaking. Checking the plant weekly rather than leaving it sealed for months makes a big difference. Where mould keeps returning, a light dusting or spray of a sulphur-based fungicide before rebagging usually settles it.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
black sooty looking stuff growing on a trap that already died, do I need fungicide

Not usually. A dead trap that has caught something is decaying organic matter, and saprophytic mould colonising it is normal rather than an infection of the living plant. Snip the dead trap off at the base and remove any old prey remains, and the mould has nothing left to feed on. If the surrounding conditions are stagnant, improve air circulation as well, since that is what lets it spread from dead tissue to healthy leaves.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Green slimy film has covered the soil in my sundew pot

That green film is algae, and it turns up where the surface stays constantly wet in bright light - it is common in tray-watered pots. It does not attack the plant, but a thick mat can seal the surface and make it harder for seedlings to establish. Scrape it off, let the top of the mix dry slightly between waterings, and a top dressing of sand or fresh live sphagnum helps keep it from returning. Never treat it with an algaecide or anything containing nutrients.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
What is this flat green leafy stuff spreading across my pot? It isn't moss exactly.

That sounds like liverwort, a flat, lobed, leathery growth that spreads in a mat over damp peat and is the bane of most carnivorous plant collections. It is not a disease but it will smother small plants and compete for the surface, so pick it off by hand as soon as you spot it and keep after the regrowth. Letting the surface dry a fraction between waterings and improving air movement both slow it down. Left alone it can take over a pot completely, so early removal is far easier than a rescue later.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
sphagnum moss is growing up over my little flytrap and burying it

Live sphagnum is generally a good sign about your water and light, but it grows faster than a small flytrap and will swallow it if you let it. Trim the moss back around the plant with scissors so the crown stays clear and gets full light, and repeat every few weeks in the growing season. There is no need to remove it all - a low carpet is fine and helps keep the surface stable. Just do not let it close over the growth point.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Grass and random weeds keep sprouting in my pitcher plant pot. Will they hurt it?

Weeds compete for light and root space and can outgrow a carnivorous plant surprisingly quickly, so pull them out while they are small. Get the roots out rather than snapping the tops off, and do it when the peat is wet so they come away cleanly without dragging your plant's roots with them. Never reach for a weedkiller or a hoe-and-feed product near these pots. Regular weeding every couple of weeks is all it takes to stay ahead.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Why are the leaves on my plant turning yellow?

Yellowing has several possible causes, so look at which leaves are affected. If it is the oldest leaves only, that is usually normal ageing and nothing to worry about. Widespread yellowing with soft growth often means the roots are struggling in soil that is waterlogged and airless, while yellowing that comes with browning tips generally points to mineral build-up from tap or bottled water. Check what you have been watering with first, then check whether the pot is draining, since those two account for most cases.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
The edges of all my leaves are going brown and crispy

Crispy brown leaf edges are the textbook sign of mineral burn from tap or bottled mineral water. Switch immediately to distilled, reverse osmosis or rainwater, then flush the pot by pouring clean mineral-free water slowly through it several times to wash the accumulated salts out of the peat. In a bad case, repot into a fresh nutrient-free mix so the plant starts clean. Existing damaged leaves will not turn green again, so judge recovery by the new growth that follows.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How do I flush a pot properly?

Take the pot out of its tray, set it somewhere it can drain freely, and pour distilled, reverse osmosis or rainwater slowly through the surface until several times the pot's volume has passed through. Repeat the flush a few times over a few days rather than doing it all in one go. The point is to carry dissolved minerals out through the drainage holes rather than leaving them concentrating in the peat. Discard the runoff and do not stand the pot back in it.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
I used bottled spring water because I thought it was pure and now the tips are all brown

Spring and mineral waters are exactly the wrong choice - the minerals are the selling point and they are what burns carnivorous plant roots. Move to distilled, reverse osmosis or collected rainwater straight away, and flush the pot by running clean water through it several times to carry the salts out. If the burn is severe or the plant is small, repot into fresh nutrient-free peat and perlite. The scorched leaves will stay brown, so watch the new growth to see whether the plant is recovering.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
My plant was fine last week and now it's just collapsed. What happened?

Sudden collapse usually traces back to something that changed recently, so retrace the last two weeks. If you repotted, it is almost certainly transplant shock, and the answer is to keep the plant humid and shaded for a week or two and wait for new growth. If you moved it into stronger light abruptly, it may be scorched, and if the soil is sodden and the plant wilting anyway, suspect root rot. A recent switch to tap water is the other common trigger.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
repotted my sarracenia and now it looks completely miserable

That is transplant shock, and it is common when roots are disturbed. Put the plant somewhere shaded and humid for a week or two, keep the medium evenly damp, and resist the urge to fuss with it further or to fertilize it. Do not judge the plant by the existing leaves, which may well brown off - what matters is whether new growth appears from the crown. Most plants pull through given a couple of quiet weeks.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Put my flytrap outside for summer and within two days it has white and brown patches

That is sunburn from too abrupt a change. A plant grown indoors has no defence against full outdoor sun, and it scorches within a day or two of being moved straight out. Bring it back to a shaded spot, then acclimate it over a week or two by giving it an hour or two of direct sun at first and steadily increasing the exposure. The scorched leaves will not repair, but new growth will come in adapted to the stronger light.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Bought a flytrap at the hardware store, it's in a sealed plastic dome. What do I do?

Those domes create hot, stagnant conditions that the plant needs to be weaned off rather than shocked out of. Open the dome a little more each day over a week or so instead of pulling it off all at once, so the plant adjusts to normal humidity. Check the soil, because these plants are often potted in an unsuitable mix - repot into a 1:1 peat and perlite blend if so, switch to distilled water, and give it as much strong light as you can. Expect a few older leaves to be lost during the transition.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
The plant I bought came in what looks like normal potting compost. Is that a problem?

It is, because ordinary potting compost contains fertilizer and the mineral salts in it will burn carnivorous plant roots over the following weeks. Repot as soon as you reasonably can into a 1:1 mix of peat and perlite with no added nutrients, rinsing as much of the old compost off the roots as you can without wrecking them. Water only with distilled, reverse osmosis or rainwater from then on. Expect a short period of sulking afterwards - that is transplant shock, and it passes.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
I neglected my flytrap for months and it's a brown mess but I think something's still alive. Can it be saved?

Quite possibly - flytraps are tougher than they look, and a firm white rhizome means there is something to work with. Trim away all the dead and blackened leaves, unpot it and check the rhizome, and repot into fresh peat and perlite if the old medium is compacted or has been watered with tap water. Set it in bright light, stand the pot in a shallow tray of mineral-free water, and leave it alone. Recovery is slow, so measure it in new leaves over the following weeks rather than day to day.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Its winter and my flytrap leaves are going black one by one. Is my plant sick or is this normal?

That is almost certainly normal dormancy rather than disease. Venus flytraps die back in winter, losing leaves and shrinking to a small low rosette, and the blackening is simply the old foliage being discarded. Trim off the dead leaves to keep mould from getting a hold, keep the soil just damp, and let the plant have its cool rest. If the rhizome stays firm, the plant is fine and will push new growth in spring.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
do sarracenia pitchers dying off in autumn mean something is wrong

No, that is the normal seasonal pattern. Sarracenia pitchers brown off as autumn comes on and the plant goes into winter dormancy, and a lot of the old growth will die back entirely. Cut the fully brown pitchers off to keep dead material from harbouring mould, but leave anything still partly green, since it is still feeding the rhizome. The plant will send up fresh pitchers in spring.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
One of my Nepenthes pitchers turned brown and dried up. Is my plant dying?

Individual pitchers have a limited lifespan and brown off one at a time - that is completely normal for Nepenthes and not a sign of illness. As long as the plant keeps producing new leaves and new pitchers, all is well. Snip off the spent ones once they are fully brown so they do not sit and rot. It would only be a concern if pitchers were browning faster than new ones form, or if the whole plant were wilting.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
my mexican pinguicula has stopped making sticky leaves and grown a weird tight little rosette

That is the normal winter succulent phase, not a problem. Mexican butterworts switch to small, non-carnivorous succulent leaves when light levels and temperatures drop, and they stay that way until spring. The important adjustment is water: during the succulent phase they need far less, and keeping them wet at that point is a very effective way to rot them. Cut back to barely damp and normal sticky leaves will return in spring.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Some of my flytrap traps go black even though the plant looks healthy. Why?

Individual traps have a working life of a few catches or a couple of months, then they blacken and die while the plant carries on making new ones. That is ordinary turnover rather than sickness, and it is the pattern that matters - a few traps blackening among healthy new growth is fine, whereas everything blackening at once is a warning. Trim off the dead traps at the base to keep decaying tissue from feeding mould. Traps also blacken faster when they close on prey that is too large to seal around.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
I fed my flytrap a big bug and the trap went black a few days later

That happens when the prey is too big for the trap to seal around it. The trap cannot form a proper airtight seal, the insect rots instead of being digested, and the trap dies off in response. Stick to prey no more than about a third of the trap's size, and remember that an outdoor plant does not need feeding at all. Cut off the blackened trap and old prey remains so they do not become a mould site.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
There are tiny white things jumping around on the surface of the soil

Those are almost certainly springtails, and they are harmless. They live on decaying organic matter in damp peat, they do not damage plants, and small carnivorous plants will happily eat them. Large numbers usually just tell you the surface is staying very wet, so letting the top dry slightly between waterings will reduce them. There is no need to spray anything for them.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
My carnivorous plant seedlings are falling over and there's white fuzz at the base

That is damping off, a fungal problem that hits seedlings kept in closed, humid, stagnant conditions. Improve airflow immediately by cracking the lid or running a small fan, remove the collapsed seedlings so the fungus has less to work with, and let the surface dry very slightly between waterings. Sowing more thinly and keeping the container out of extreme warmth helps prevent it. A sulphur-based fungicide is worth applying if it keeps spreading.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
When should I actually reach for a fungicide?

Fungicide is the follow-up, not the first move. Start by fixing what caused the outbreak - stagnant air, a permanently sodden surface, dead leaves and old prey left to decay in a closed container - because in most cases that alone clears it up. If mould persists after air circulation is improved and dead material removed, a sulphur-based fungicide is the usual choice among carnivorous plant growers. Check the label and reject anything that also contains fertilizer.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Is my Cephalotus at risk of rot? Mine sits in a water tray like my flytrap does.

Take it out of the tray - Cephalotus is one of the genera most prone to root rot, along with Nepenthes and Mexican butterworts in their winter succulent phase. Flytraps and Sarracenia are bog plants that tolerate standing water, but Cephalotus wants an open mix that drains and dries slightly between waterings. Water from the top and let the excess run out rather than letting the pot sit in it. Root rot comes from soil that is both waterlogged and airless, so drainage and air in the mix are what protect it.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How do I tell fungus gnats from thrips? Both are tiny and I can't see properly.

Fungus gnats are dark mosquito-like flies that take off from the soil surface when you disturb the pot, and they are mainly a soil-dwelling nuisance. Thrips are much narrower, more slender and slower, live on the plant rather than the soil, and leave silvery scarring and distorted new growth behind them. The damage tells you as much as the insect does: if the soil swarms but the leaves look fine it is gnats, and if new growth is scarred and deformed it is thrips. Thrips need repeated insecticidal soap treatments about a week apart, while gnats mostly respond to drying the surface and sticky traps.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Can I just use the bug spray from the garden centre that I use on my roses?

Check the label very carefully before you do. Many general garden sprays are combined pest-and-feed formulations, and the fertilizer in them will burn carnivorous plant roots even if the insecticide itself is harmless. If it contains no added nutrients, test it on one leaf and wait a day or two before treating the whole plant, since carnivorous plants are more sensitive to sprays than roses are. For most household infestations, plain insecticidal soap or submerging the plant in distilled water is a safer and equally effective route.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
i sprayed my plant for aphids two weeks ago and they're back

That is normal and it does not mean the spray failed. Soap sprays kill the insects present but do not kill eggs, so a fresh generation hatches out days later and it looks like the problem returned. The fix is to plan on repeat treatments roughly a week apart for two or three rounds instead of a single spray. Check the growth point and leaf undersides each time, since that is where survivors hide.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Plant looks green and healthy but it hasn't made a single new trap in ages. Any ideas?

Healthy foliage with no new traps almost always points to insufficient light - carnivorous plants need strong, direct light to invest in traps at all. Give it the brightest spot you have, or a strong grow light, and move it outdoors gradually over a week or two if you plan to summer it outside. Also confirm it has had a proper winter dormancy if it is a flytrap or Sarracenia, since a plant denied that rest slowly weakens and stops producing. Do not be tempted to fertilize the soil to encourage growth - that will do damage, not good.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Should I be cutting off dead leaves or just leaving them?

Cut them off. Dead leaves and the remains of digested prey are the food source that mould and rot start from, and removing them is one of the simplest preventive things you can do. Trim fully brown or black leaves back to the base with clean scissors, but leave anything still partly green, since the plant is still drawing from it. Do this alongside keeping the air moving and the surface slightly drier between waterings and most fungal trouble never gets started.
